title: Equivalence classes of finite-time transitions in optimal control and non-equilibrium relaxation
authors: Jan Meibohm, Samuel Monter, Clemens Bechinger, Sarah A. M. Loos
abstract: We present a theory for the optimal control of stochastic systems in structured environments, represented by penalty terms in the cost functional. We show that such control problems generically feature sharp finite-time transitions associated with a qualitative change in the control strategy at a critical time. Starting from an overdamped Langevin equation and a quadratic cost functional, we show that all resulting problems fall into three canonical equivalence classes (parabolic, hyperbolic, and elliptic), distinguished by the sign of the determinant of the control Hamiltonian. For each class, we obtain the optimal protocol, the cost function, and the critical time in closed form, and show that the transition exhibits features of a continuous phase transition at mean-field level. We then establish a mapping between the optimal control cost and the large-deviation rate function governing non-equilibrium relaxation after a potential quench. The mapping covers the parabolic and hyperbolic classes, while the elliptic class has no simple relaxation counterpart. This correspondence implies that recently discovered finite-time dynamical phase transitions, which are exponentially costly to sample directly, are accessible through ordinary averages over optimally controlled trajectories. To validate our theoretical findings, we report three experiments with optically trapped colloidal particles: a control transition for the mean stochastic work, and the finite-time dynamical phase transitions in free diffusion and in harmonic relaxation.
summary: This work provides a unified theoretical framework for analyzing optimal control of stochastic systems, classifying the resulting problems into three mathematical types. It establishes a deep connection between the minimum cost required for optimal control and the rate function governing non-equilibrium relaxation after a quench. The theory is validated through experiments on colloidal particles, demonstrating access to rare-event physics via controlled trajectories.
main_problem: The paper develops a theory for optimally controlling stochastic systems in structured environments, focusing on identifying and characterizing sharp finite-time transitions.
main_result: The control problems are classified into three canonical equivalence classes (parabolic, hyperbolic, elliptic), and the optimal control cost is shown to map to the large-deviation rate function governing non-equilibrium relaxation for two of these classes.
method: The authors use optimal control theory (Pontryagin's principle) applied to an overdamped Langevin equation, linearizing the dynamics around a fixed point to classify the resulting mathematical structure.
model_or_system: The system is modeled by an overdamped Langevin equation, analyzed in the context of optimal control cost minimization and non-equilibrium relaxation following a potential quench. Experiments are validated using optically trapped colloidal particles.
key_observables: Optimal protocols, cost functions, critical times ($t_c$), and the large-deviation rate function.
important_parameters: Friction coefficient ($\gamma$), trap stiffness ($\kappa$), and the dimensionless noise parameter ($\epsilon$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on linearizing the dynamics around a zero-control fixed point, and the mapping between control cost and rate function fails for the elliptic class.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the control transition for mean stochastic work (parabolic class) and the finite-time dynamical phase transitions in free diffusion and harmonic relaxation.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the general theory by classifying control problems into three classes based on the control Hamiltonian determinant. It then derives explicit solutions for the optimal protocol and cost for each class, establishing the mapping to non-equilibrium relaxation theory, and finally validates these findings with three distinct experiments on colloidal particles.
why_interesting: The connection drawn between finite-time dynamical phase transitions (a non-equilibrium concept) and the cost of optimal control provides a powerful, measurable tool to probe rare-event physics in open quantum or mesoscopic systems.
